title: Scalable elimination or permanent silencing of persistent viral genomes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a safe, scalable treatment that removes persistent viral genetic material or keeps it inactive for the long term, allowing people to stop suppressive antivirals without renewed disease. Persistent reservoirs are infected cells or tissues in which viral genomes survive treatment and can later restart infection. HIV transplantation studies and HSV reservoir-editing experiments provide different proofs of principle, but neither establishes a broadly usable clinical solution.

Conceptual synthesis: elimination and permanent silencing are distinct routes to this goal. Elimination seeks to remove or irreversibly disable genomes capable of producing infectious virus. Silencing could leave such genomes in place while preventing clinically relevant viral activity and infectious shedding. A reversible period of latency is insufficient: the intended advance is durable control without continuing suppressive treatment, although finite observation cannot establish literal lifetime permanence.

Conceptual synthesis: the intended scope includes integrated reservoirs, exemplified by HIV provirus embedded in host DNA, and episomal reservoirs, in which viral DNA persists separately from host chromosomes. HBV and herpesviruses are proposed targets for the latter class, but their reservoir biology should not be treated as interchangeable. Genome editing, durable regulation of viral activity, and controlled reactivation followed by clearance are possible approaches rather than demonstrated components of one universal treatment.

significance.text: A successful intervention would change the treatment goal from continuing suppression to a finite course that produces drug-free remission. For HIV, effective antiretroviral therapy suppresses replication, but stopping it usually permits rebound. For HSV, conventional antivirals reduce symptoms and transmission without eliminating latent infection in ganglionic neurons. Removing the need for continuing suppression would therefore be a major advance even if it did not reverse all damage caused before treatment.

Reduced transmission is a conditional downstream benefit, not an automatic consequence of lower viral DNA measurements. It would require suppression of infectious shedding, sufficient treatment uptake, and durable effectiveness in the relevant populations. Aubert and colleagues connect latent HSV-1 DNA targeting with reduced induced shedding in mice, but the relationship between human HSV shedding quantity and transmission probability remains incompletely understood.

HIV remission after allogeneic transplantation shows that prolonged treatment-free control is biologically possible in selected patients with haematological cancer. It does not prove complete reservoir clearance or identify a single sufficient clearance mechanism. Transplantation is therefore a proof of principle whose risks, eligibility restrictions, and resource demands prevent it from serving as the proposed population-scale solution.

Impact synthesis: ending ongoing viral activity would not necessarily reverse established cancer, tissue injury, or autoimmune disease. Those outcomes require separate evidence. In particular, whether interrupting a persistent infection reverses a major chronic disease remains the distinct question represented by VIR-11. The revolutionary claim here concerns durable reservoir control and freedom from suppressive treatment, rather than guaranteed reversal of every consequence of infection.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is reliable control of the clinically relevant reservoir throughout the body at an acceptable risk. HIV can persist despite effective suppression, while latent HSV occupies ganglionic neurons. In the HSV editing study, effects differed substantially across ganglia and treatment regimens. These findings make delivery coverage and residual reactivatable virus concrete barriers; they do not establish that every editor or silencer necessarily misses reservoir cells.

Mechanistic synthesis: approaches that reactivate virus and then clear infected cells, often called shock and kill, must couple reactivation to effective clearance. Approaches that reinforce inactivity, often called block and lock, must prevent subsequent escape from silencing. The supplied evidence does not establish a single latency switch shared by HIV, herpesviruses, and HBV, or a complete molecular program that can be manipulated to deliver either outcome across these infections. Understanding regulation is useful only if it leads to durable control in the relevant cells and tissues.

Delivery and potency must be improved without exchanging viral disease for treatment injury. Aubert and colleagues observed liver toxicity and histological neuronal injury with some mouse regimens. A clinical platform must therefore address vector toxicity, tissue injury, immune effects, and potential host-genome damage, while preserving the function of long-lived infected cells where their destruction would be harmful.

A further barrier is distinguishing a greatly reduced reservoir from one that can no longer restart infection. Gaebler and colleagues could not rule out persistent intact HIV despite extensive negative sampling. A retained abstract from the 2023 NIH Strategies for an HIV Cure meeting likewise described rebound within six weeks of treatment interruption in participants selected for low reservoir measurements, including situations in which intact virus was not detected. That abstract is conference evidence, retained in a partially extracted meeting book, and should not be confused with TAG's later trial listing.

Engineering synthesis: avoiding transplantation is necessary for the proposed scope but does not itself establish scalability. A usable intervention must have feasible manufacturing, reproducible delivery, sufficiently broad eligibility, and resource requirements compatible with treating people who may already do well on existing drugs. A platform may need virus-specific components rather than one identical intervention for every reservoir class.

current_state.text: HIV transplantation: Gaebler and colleagues' Nature report, identified in the research notes as published on 1 December 2025, describes more than six years of remission after allogeneic transplantation involving heterozygous CCR5Δ32 in a patient treated for acute myeloid leukaemia. Plasma HIV RNA remained undetectable, and no replication-competent virus was recovered from sampled blood or intestinal tissues. The authors nevertheless could not exclude persistent intact HIV elsewhere or below assay detection limits. Their reference to six previously documented cures describes the context of that report, not a verified current worldwide count.

HIV clinical development: Treatment Action Group's listing dated 16 October 2026 states that none of its listed studies is expected to produce a cure. It identifies EBT-101 as a CRISPR/Cas9 intervention targeting HIV provirus, trial NCT05144386, and supplies conference references. This is a dated description of the listed research and TAG's expectations, not evidence that no intervention anywhere could achieve remission.

The research notes describe EBT-101 as AAV-delivered and attribute to 2024 conference journalism early safety observations in a handful of participants, rebound in everyone who interrupted therapy, and delayed rebound in one participant. They identify aidsmap coverage dated 14 May 2024 and POZ coverage dated 31 July 2024. Neither article's text was retained for the supplied review, and no peer-reviewed trial report was supplied. These clinical details therefore remain attributed reports that cannot be independently assessed from this package; the missing material does not establish that the reports are false or that no peer-reviewed publication exists.

HBV: the research notes attribute to Hou and colleagues a bepirovirsen trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 28 May 2026, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2515131. They report functional cure, described as sustained HBV DNA suppression plus HBsAg loss, in 127 of 650 patients, approximately 20%, and 106 of 570 patients, approximately 19%, versus none on placebo. The notes describe participants as non-cirrhotic, already receiving nucleos(t)ide analogues, and having baseline HBsAg greater than 100 through 3000 IU/mL. No trial text or retained artifact was supplied to verify the counts, denominators, eligibility criteria, endpoint timing, or treatment-withdrawal conditions. These figures are preserved as an unverified research-note report, not as an established result of this record. Even if confirmed, the reported functional-cure endpoint would not demonstrate cccDNA clearance.

The research also cites a November 2026 Antiviral Research review concerning HBV cccDNA and integrated DNA as obstacles to cure. Its text and author list were not retained, so its identity and attributed conclusion could not be verified in the supplied review. It cannot resolve the missing trial details or establish that bepirovirsen eliminates either form of persistent DNA.

HSV-1 editing: Aubert and colleagues' Nature Communications study, published on 13 May 2024, reports large reductions in latent HSV-1 DNA in mice using meganuclease therapy. Some experiments achieved reductions of 90% or more. In the genital-infection model, the reported reduction was 97.7% in dorsal root ganglia, based on four treated and seven control mice; other ganglia showed smaller reductions. This is a tissue-specific mouse result, not removal of 97.7% of every reservoir throughout an animal or a demonstration in humans.

The HSV study found a significant pooled reduction in pharmacologically induced shedding, while individual experiments were often nonsignificant and genital shedding observations were too sparse for meaningful statistical analysis. Residual virus could still reactivate in some treated groups, but partial reservoir reduction did not invariably produce observed shedding: one experiment found none in eight treated mice. Neither finding establishes permanent cure. The study also reported hepatotoxicity in 7 of 70 high-dose animals and histological neuronal injury with some regimens. It does not demonstrate human whole-body reservoir eradication; its discussion of a small human keratitis study does not establish that outcome either.

Evidence scope: the supplied review assessed retained article text for the HIV transplantation and HSV studies, but did not visually inspect their figures or linked supplements. Some associated PDFs had missing extractable text or extraction warnings. The 2023 meeting book was only partially retained, although the cited rebound abstract was available. The package provides dated findings and an October 2026 HIV trial snapshot; its empty freshness record does not establish comprehensive field-wide status as of 1 November 2026 or later.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a safe intervention platform, without allogeneic transplantation, should produce multi-year remission after suppressive antivirals stop. Demonstrating this in an integrated retrovirus and an episomal DNA virus would provide convincing breadth for the stated concept. These are proposed criteria, not established scientific standards. Success in two reservoir classes would establish performance in those tested settings, not universality across persistent viruses.
completion_criteria.label: Safe nontransplant multi-year remission across integrated and episomal viruses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed endpoint distinction: an elimination claim should require no recoverable replication-competent virus across explicitly stated tissues, sampling schedules, assay sensitivities, and follow-up periods. A permanent-silencing claim may allow retained replication-competent genomes, but should require durable absence of clinically relevant viral activity and infectious shedding. Neither negative sampling nor finite follow-up can prove that no competent genome remains anywhere or that reactivation is impossible for life.
completion_criteria.label: Elimination excludes recoverable virus; silencing prevents activity and shedding

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional testing: where clinically appropriate, monitored treatment interruption should establish whether control persists without suppressive drugs, with virus-specific surveillance, stopping rules, and rescue treatment. Reservoir DNA measurements should support this demonstration rather than substitute for it. The rationale is grounded in prolonged remission assessed alongside reservoir assays in the transplantation study and the conference report of rebound despite very low reservoir measurements.
completion_criteria.label: Monitored treatment interruption demonstrates sustained control without suppressive drugs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and safety demonstration: results should recur in independent clinical cohorts and centres, with transparent reporting of treatment failures, rebound timing, shedding, and relevant tissue measurements. Follow-up should assess host-genome damage, vector toxicity, immune effects, and organ or neuronal injury. Acceptable risk should be judged against the benefits and burdens of existing treatment, including for people otherwise stable on suppressive drugs; no numerical safety threshold is established here.
completion_criteria.label: Independent clinical cohorts reproduce remission with transparent safety reporting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: scalability should be shown through reproducible manufacturing and delivery, defined eligibility, feasible treatment and monitoring requirements, and explicit resource demands. Studies should identify the virus types, reservoir locations, and patient groups for which effectiveness has actually been demonstrated. A molecular map of latency, a large DNA reduction, or success in a narrowly selected transplant recipient would be an enabling result rather than completion of this clinical capability.
completion_criteria.label: Scalability demonstrated with explicit resource demands and effectiveness limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — VIR-01, A prospective sequence-to-phenotype theory of infectivity, transmission, and escape: predictive understanding could help anticipate viral escape from reservoir-targeting interventions and interpret residual virus. VIR-01 concerns prediction from sequence; VIR-03 requires durable control of an established reservoir in people.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-02, Empiric medicines that cover the major causes of severe acute viral disease: broad acute antivirals could complement reservoir treatment by controlling active replication. Their central objective is empiric treatment of severe acute disease, whereas VIR-03 addresses persistence after ordinary suppression has left a reservoir intact.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-04, Protective immunity that covers a viral family, including future variants and unseen relatives: broad immunity could help prevent infection or contribute to control after a reservoir intervention. Protection across a viral family does not itself demonstrate elimination or permanent silencing of an existing persistent infection.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-05, Durable immunity at the respiratory surface that stops transmission: both concepts could reduce transmission, but their targets differ. VIR-05 seeks durable protection at a respiratory entry and shedding surface; VIR-03 targets established persistent genomes and must separately demonstrate effects on infectious shedding.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-06, Bacteriophage therapy that can be prescribed as reliably as an antibacterial drug: both involve making biologically complex interventions reliable enough for routine prescribing. VIR-06 uses viruses to treat bacterial infection; it does not address persistent viral reservoirs in human cells.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-07, Viral particles that can be aimed at chosen human cells, given again, and carry large genes: selective delivery, repeat administration, and payload capacity could enable reservoir-directed editors or silencers. Delivery is an enabling capability, while VIR-03 additionally requires durable clinical control, adequate reservoir coverage, and acceptable safety.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-08, A general experimental reading of viral genes that have no recognizable relatives: discovering unknown viral gene functions could reveal persistence mechanisms or treatment targets. Functional interpretation of genes is distinct from demonstrating that a treatment eliminates or silences reservoirs in people.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-09, A mechanistic correlate that predicts human protection from a new virus: mechanistic measures of protection could inform immune contributions to durable reservoir control. Predicting protection from a new virus and establishing treatment-free control of an existing infection remain different endpoints; a protection correlate cannot replace a reservoir or rebound assessment.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-10, A single-dose, conditionally replicating interfering particle that keeps a chronic virus suppressed: this overlaps directly with the goal of avoiding repeated conventional treatment. Continued suppression by an active interfering particle would not by itself establish reservoir elimination or permanent silencing. The distinction depends on what maintains control and whether persistent genomes remain capable of restarting disease.

Roster-based synthesis — VIR-11, An interruptible causal chain from a persistent virus to a major chronic disease: reservoir elimination or silencing could provide a way to interrupt an implicated infection. VIR-11 separately requires causal evidence connecting that infection to disease and evidence that intervention changes the disease course. Success under VIR-03 would not automatically establish reversal of autoimmunity, cancer, or prior tissue injury.

change_log.change: Separated elimination from permanent silencing and aligned their endpoints.
change_log.reason: Silencing may retain replication-competent genomes, so absence of such genomes cannot be required for both routes.

change_log.change: Replaced the implied common latency switch and universal delivery failure with specific mechanistic and delivery barriers.
change_log.reason: The reviewed sources establish persistence and variable reservoir targeting, but not one shared switch across HIV, HSV, and HBV or failure of every editor and silencer.

change_log.change: Qualified the HIV transplantation result as prolonged remission with negative sampled assays rather than proven whole-body eradication.
change_log.reason: The study explicitly cannot exclude persistent intact HIV. Its six-case introductory count is historical context, not a current global total.

change_log.change: Retained EBT-101 safety and rebound details as attributed, unverified reports.
change_log.reason: The cited journalism was not retained, and TAG's listing identifies the intervention and conference references without establishing those clinical outcomes.

change_log.change: Preserved the HBV numerical results, eligibility details, and publication information with explicit research-note attribution.
change_log.reason: No trial artifact was supplied. Missing evidence warrants qualification rather than deletion or a conclusion that the result is false.

change_log.change: Distinguished reported HBV functional cure from demonstrated cccDNA clearance.
change_log.reason: DNA suppression and HBsAg loss do not establish elimination of the persistent DNA reservoir.

change_log.change: Specified the HSV-1 mouse model, 97.7% dorsal-root-ganglion reduction, group sizes, and variation across tissues.
change_log.reason: The original wording could imply uniform or whole-body reservoir removal.

change_log.change: Added shedding-analysis limitations, hepatotoxicity in 7 of 70 high-dose animals, and histological neuronal injury.
change_log.reason: These details materially affect interpretation of efficacy and clinical feasibility.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that partial reductions always rebound with a conditional reactivation statement.
change_log.reason: Some treated groups shed virus, while one experiment observed no shedding in eight treated mice; neither establishes universal rebound or permanent cure.

change_log.change: Separated direct remission benefits from conditional transmission effects and chronic-disease reversal.
change_log.reason: Transmission depends on infectious shedding and uptake, while reversal of established disease requires separate evidence.

change_log.change: Omitted the HCV historical comparison and broad papillomavirus assertion from the factual explanation.
change_log.reason: The supplied review found no inspected support for those additions; neither is necessary to preserve the concept's identity or significance.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to include reproducibility, assay limits, route-specific endpoints, practical scalability, and comparative safety.
change_log.reason: Excluding transplantation alone does not establish scalability, and finite clinical tests cannot prove lifetime permanence or universality.

change_log.change: Identified the 2023 conference meeting book separately from TAG's October 2026 listing and preserved extraction and freshness limits.
change_log.reason: The source entry contains different documents with different evidentiary roles, and the supplied package does not support a comprehensive current-field assessment.

change_log.change: Explained connections and distinctions for every other entry in the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: Related enabling capabilities and clinical goals should remain separate concepts rather than being merged into reservoir elimination.

unresolved_issues: The Hou et al. bepirovirsen trial text is absent. Its reported counts, eligibility, endpoint timing, treatment-withdrawal conditions, and publication details remain unverified within the supplied package.
The cited November 2026 HBV review has no retained text or author list; its identity and attributed conclusion remain unresolved.
The EBT-101 journalism and a peer-reviewed clinical trial report were not supplied. Safety, participant outcomes, delayed rebound, and publication status cannot be resolved here.

The supplied evidence does not establish a shared latency mechanism across HIV, herpesviruses, and HBV, or determine whether one common platform can safely control both integrated and episomal reservoirs.
The duration and breadth of follow-up needed for a persuasive permanent-silencing claim remain proposed judgments; lifetime permanence cannot be proven by finite observation.
Whole-body reservoir coverage and residual replication competence remain uncertain when tissue sampling and assay sensitivity are limited.
The research notes date the HIV Nature publication to 1 December 2025 while listing it in volume 650; the supplied review does not reconcile online-publication and issue dates.
Figures and linked supplements were not visually inspected in the supplied review, some PDFs had extraction limitations, and the 2023 meeting-book extraction was truncated.
The empty freshness record prevents a comprehensive field-wide status claim as of 1 November 2026 or later.

The review's recommendation to omit unsupported HBV and EBT-101 outcome details was not adopted as outright deletion. Those details were retained with explicit attribution and evidence limitations to preserve useful research content without presenting it as verified.

The original requirement for one intervention across two reservoir classes was interpreted as one intervention platform potentially using virus-specific components. Whether an identical treatment across both classes is necessary or feasible remains unresolved.

brief.title: Lasting freedom from treatment for persistent viruses
possible: People living with persistent viral infections could finish treatment and stay well without continuing drugs that keep the virus suppressed. Treatment would remove hidden viral genetic material or keep it inactive for the long term.
why: For people with HIV or herpes, this would change treatment from ongoing suppression to a finite course. It would address the hidden infection that can restart when current medicines stop.

sources.showed: A man with HIV remained free of viral rebound after stopping suppressive drugs following a donor stem cell transplant for leukaemia.
sources.quote: So far, HIV remission has been sustained for more than 6 years with undetectable plasma HIV RNA.
sources.cited_for: Long-lasting HIV control without suppressive drugs is biologically possible.
sources.not_established: This selected cancer patient's outcome does not establish complete viral removal or a treatment suitable for broad use.

sources.showed: Gene editing, which changes DNA, greatly reduced hidden herpes DNA in small mouse experiments. It also reduced virus released after drug-induced reactivation.
sources.quote: Using a pharmacological approach to reactivate latent HSV-1, we demonstrate that ganglionic viral load reduction leads to a significant decrease of viral shedding in treated female mice.
sources.cited_for: Targeting hidden herpes DNA can reduce both its amount and subsequent viral release in mice.
sources.not_established: The experiments did not establish a permanent cure or human effectiveness; some regimens caused liver and nerve-cell injury.

sources.showed: This review concerns persistent hepatitis B DNA as an obstacle to cure.
sources.cited_for: Persistent hepatitis B DNA is a barrier that cure strategies must address.
sources.not_established: A review of these barriers does not demonstrate their removal by a treatment.

sources.showed: The group lists clinical studies working toward an HIV cure and states that none of the listed studies is expected to produce one.
sources.cited_for: Clinical research is testing routes toward HIV cure.
sources.not_established: A trial listing does not demonstrate lasting control without suppressive drugs.

sources.showed: This is conference reporting on an early human study of gene editing against HIV.
sources.cited_for: Gene editing against persistent HIV has reached human testing.
sources.not_established: Early human testing does not establish durable control without suppressive drugs.

sources.showed: This is conference reporting on an early human study of gene editing against HIV.
sources.cited_for: Gene editing against persistent HIV has reached human testing.
sources.not_established: Early human testing does not establish durable control without suppressive drugs.

shown: Gaebler and colleagues documented more than six years of HIV control without suppressive drugs after a transplant for leukaemia. Aubert and colleagues reduced hidden herpes DNA and induced viral release in mice. These are separate proofs of principle; neither provides a broadly usable treatment.
missing: A treatment must reach hidden virus throughout the relevant tissues and prevent the remaining virus from restarting infection.
Effective delivery must avoid unacceptable damage to DNA, organs and nerve cells.
Clinical studies must demonstrate lasting control after suppressive drugs stop, followed by reproducible manufacturing and delivery.

milestones.label: Safe remission across different forms of hidden viral DNA
milestones.explanation: A safe platform without donor transplantation would have to sustain remission for years in viruses whose DNA sits inside host DNA and viruses whose DNA stays separate. This would establish breadth across the tested settings.

milestones.label: Clear evidence of removal or lasting inactivity
milestones.explanation: Removal would require no recoverable virus capable of reproducing under defined testing; silencing would require lasting absence of harmful activity and infectious viral release. These distinguish the routes to lasting control.

milestones.label: Sustained control after suppressive drugs stop
milestones.explanation: Where appropriate, monitored pauses with virus-specific checks and rescue treatment would have to demonstrate continued control. Low viral DNA measurements alone cannot establish freedom from treatment.

milestones.label: Repeated clinical success with transparent safety results
milestones.explanation: Independent patient groups and centres would have to reproduce remission while reporting failures, viral return, viral release and treatment injury. This would establish reliability and risk relative to existing care.

milestones.label: Practical treatment with clearly defined reach
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to establish reproducible production and delivery, eligibility, monitoring needs, resource demands and effectiveness limits. This would establish whether treatment could reach people beyond exceptional cases.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether a common treatment platform can safely control these different forms of persistent viral DNA.
Limited tissue sampling can miss virus that remains capable of restarting infection.
The follow-up needed to support permanent silencing remains unsettled; finite observation cannot prove lifelong inactivity.

page.title: Elimination or silencing of persistent viral reservoirs
page.definition: A finite treatment eliminates or silences viral DNA reservoirs, infected cells retaining genetic material that can restart infection, so control persists after suppressive antivirals stop. This excludes cure requiring allogeneic stem-cell transplantation; remission alone does not establish permanent silencing.

goal.need: In most people with HIV, viraemia returns within 4 weeks of stopping antiretroviral therapy. Most people starting hepatitis B treatment require lifelong therapy; only 4.3% of people with chronic HBV received antivirals in 2024. A finite curative treatment would remove the continuing requirement for suppression.

figures.note: The infection count includes people who do not meet treatment eligibility criteria.

statements.quote: The aim is to drive concerted efforts to accelerate global scientific research and engagement towards a cure for HIV.
The cure should provide an individual with at least 2 years of effective virus control.
statements.context: This concerns the minimum HIV combination-therapy profile. Table 2 specifies HIV RNA <200 copies/mL, effectiveness in ≥20% of recipients, average relapse <10% per year and remission >2 years. Its target population is healthy, virologically suppressed adults aged >16 and <65 years, receiving stable antiretroviral therapy, with CD4 counts >500 cells/µL.

statements.body: AASLD–EASL HBV-HDV Treatment Endpoints Conference Faculty
statements.quote: If we cannot safely and easily achieve elimination of cccDNA, the next best goal would be silencing (or degradation) of cccDNA
statements.context: cccDNA is covalently closed circular HBV DNA retained separately from host chromosomes. The panel recommends a clinical functional-cure endpoint of HBsAg loss, using an assay with a 0.05 IU/mL detection limit, and HBV DNA <10 IU/mL at 24 weeks off therapy. This differs from complete cure.

statements.quote: Identify candidates for elimination of virus or functional cure
statements.context: The passage concerns HSV in Priority 3 of the proposed strategic framework circulated for public comment.

completion.title: A finite treatment is licensed for cure through elimination or silencing of a persistent viral reservoir.
completion.criterion: For one named virus, FDA grants marketing authorisation to a finite treatment, without allogeneic haematopoietic transplantation, whose approved indication and assessment establish sustained treatment-free control through elimination or silencing of its persistent reservoir. The accepted clinical endpoints, eligible population, response rate and follow-up are those in that assessment. Approval for suppression or an off-treatment biomarker response alone does not establish the reservoir claim.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational criterion; no shared cross-virus completion standard was found.
completion.basis: Searches of IAS/Sunnylands HIV cure profiles, AASLD–EASL HBV guidance, NIH HSV priorities and FDA approval rules found no shared test for permanent silencing or scalability. Authorisation with an established reservoir claim is the Atlas proxy. HIV remission beyond 6 years in one stem-cell recipient establishes biological possibility outside this scope. Bepirovirsen's approval on 20 October 2026 establishes HBV clinical progress, not persistent-DNA elimination.

milestones.title: A reservoir-directed candidate demonstrates biological activity in a nonclinical model.
milestones.criterion: Nonclinical evidence establishes biological plausibility and biological activity in a relevant model; FDA specifies no universal reservoir-reduction percentage. On 13 May 2024, Aubert et al. reported 97.7% less HSV-1 DNA in dorsal-root ganglia of 4 treated versus 7 control mice, and reduced induced shedding in pooled experiments. These results do not establish eradication; hepatotoxicity occurred in 7 of 70 high-dose mice.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Preclinical Assessment of Investigational Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, section III.A. This guidance covers cell and gene therapy approaches to each infection.

milestones.title: A reservoir-directed candidate reaches initial administration and safety assessment in people.
milestones.criterion: First human administration and initial safety assessment occur under a clinical protocol. At AIDS 2024, held from 22 July 2024 to 26 July 2024, EBT-101 investigators reported no serious adverse events in 6 participants; all 3 interrupting HIV treatment rebounded (not peer reviewed). On 31 August 2023, Wei et al. reported ocular HSV-1 editing in 3 people during corneal transplantation, with no keratitis recurrence over 14, 18 and 21 months. Neuronal-reservoir clearance was not established.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a), defining initial human investigation. This stage establishes human exposure, not curative efficacy.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans

milestones.title: A controlled clinical study finds preliminary efficacy for a reservoir-directed treatment.
milestones.criterion: A controlled phase 2 study provides preliminary evidence of efficacy for its intended indication; the regulation sets no universal response-rate cutoff. B-Clear, published on 8 November 2022, enrolled 457 adults. Its endpoint was HBsAg <0.05 IU/mL and HBV DNA <20 IU/mL maintained for 24 weeks after bepirovirsen stopped, without newly initiated antivirals. This occurred in 6/68 participants continuing background antivirals and 7/70 not receiving them in the 24-week treatment groups. HBsAg is hepatitis B surface antigen.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b–c), defining controlled phase 2 investigation and preliminary effectiveness before phase 3; B-Clear's numerical endpoint applies only to HBV.

milestones.title: Pivotal studies establish efficacy and characterise the benefit–risk of a reservoir-directed treatment.
milestones.criterion: Pivotal studies establish efficacy and characterise benefit–risk for the intended indication. B-Well 1/2, published on 28 May 2026, studied noncirrhotic adults receiving background antivirals, with baseline HBsAg >100 to 3000 IU/mL. At week 72, functional cure occurred in 127/650 versus 0/328 and 106/570 versus 0/286 participants. The endpoint required HBsAg <0.05 IU/mL, HBV DNA <20 IU/mL and no rescue therapy, 24 weeks after background antivirals stopped; isolated blips were permitted. These endpoints do not establish reservoir elimination.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(c), defining the evidence sought in phase 3; the B-Well numerical endpoint applies only to HBV.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate the overall benefit-risk relationship of the drug
